To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the glass transition temperature decreases with film thickness below 10 nm, (2) the thermal expansivity in the glassy region decreases with thickness while that in the molten region does not, and (3) these results can be explained in terms of the surface glass transition temperature and the thickness dependence of the bulk glass transition temperature.

the glass transition of ultrathin PS films is independent of thickness and that the thermal expansivities of both the molten and the glassy states of ultrathin films are smaller than those of bulk films.
the T(g) decreases as the film thickness decreases, and the thermal expansivity in the glassy and molten states decreases as the film becomes thinner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the thermal expansion behavior of ultrahigh vacuum (UHV)-deposited polymer thin films.
the thermal expansion behavior of ultrahin polymer films supported by silicon substrate.
the thermal expansion behavior of PS ultrathin films, focusing on the glass transition temperature and the expansivity of ultrathin films.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the thermal expansivities in the molten and glassy states decrease with decreasing film thickness.
T(g) decreases and thermal expansivity decreases in the glassy and molten states with decreasing thickness, and these behaviors are well reproduced by the two-layer model.
ultrathin PS films exhibit a unique thermal expansion behavior, which is different from that of bulk PS and ultrathin films of other polymers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the surface T(g) is almost independent of film thickness while the surface expansivity is reduced with thickness in the molten and glassy states.
the glassy state is more strongly influenced by the interface than the molten state, which may be related to the surface T(g).
the surface T(g) is lower than the bulk T(g), the surface T(g ) is constant at 354.5 +/- 0.5 K, and the thermal expansivity of the surface is smaller than the bulk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the thermal expansivities of the glassy and molten states are not constant but decrease with decreasing thickness.
the thermal expansivities of the surface layer and the bulk layer in the glassy and molten states are almost identical.
the thermal expansion of ultrathin films is not simply determined by the film thickness and the surface T(g) is almost independent of film thickness, at least for the system studied.
